issues.item: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
issues.explanation: 'Threat in Delays' suggests a broad expectancy of external danger from uncertainty/delays, which fits poorly with the stated trauma type of accidentally causing serious injury to another; the rest of the profile centers on guilt, recall-based distress, and hypervigilance rather than delay-specific threat meanings.

issues.item: Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body
issues.explanation: 'Body Unreliable' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma type. For a patient whose trauma was accidentally injuring another, the appraisals presented otherwise focus on guilt, inadequacy, and permanent moral/personal change. A loss of trust in one's body usually implies prominent bodily injury, dissociation, panic-like symptoms, or functional impairment, none of which are represented elsewhere in Triggers, Memory, Threat, or Strategies.

vignette:
Martin had been 62 for less than a year when he finally agreed to speak at length about the night that had altered the shape of his life. He was an American man of European background, married for more than three decades, and had spent most of his working life as a bank teller in a quiet suburban branch where the days were ordinarily defined by routine, small talk, and the soft clatter of coins. The event he returned to was not a criminal assault or a disaster but an accident he had caused himself, and that fact appeared to trouble him as much as the injury that followed. One evening, after a long and stressful day at the bank and at home, he was reversing his car out of a driveway when he struck a neighbor who had stepped behind the vehicle unexpectedly. The man fell hard and sustained a serious injury. Martin described the moment with a strained, stuttering precision, as if he were trying to hold the scene still long enough to understand it. He remembered the sound of the impact, the sudden realization that it was not an object he had hit, and then the neighbor's distress. When he tried to recall it now, he said, the same terror came back into his body, not just the facts of what happened. At times fragments of the memory arrived without warning - the jolt, the look on the other man's face, the feeling of being trapped in the instant - and disappeared just as quickly, leaving him shaken and disoriented.

In the weeks and months that followed, Martin found himself increasingly uneasy around people he knew, especially those connected to the event. A conversation with that neighbor, a mention of the family, or even an ordinary encounter with someone from the same circle could make him tense immediately, as though something irreversible were about to be said. He became especially uneasy when he was under stress at work. The bank was never loud, but during busy periods he noticed that his shoulders would rise and his attention would narrow, and he would feel as though he could not afford to let his guard slip. He began to notice that unexpected touch unsettled him in a way that felt out of proportion to the moment itself. If a coworker brushed his arm while passing behind him at the counter, or if his wife touched him without warning while he was absorbed in thought, he would flinch internally and need a moment to recover his composure. He would not describe himself as panicked, but he was aware of a quick, sharp alarm that made him feel exposed.

Martin said that his sense of danger had extended into the night. He had difficulty falling asleep because, even in bed beside his wife, he felt he needed to stay alert. He would lie there listening for sounds in the house, watching the bedroom door, telling himself that he should be able to relax in his own room but finding that he could not. He described being superalert or watchful or on guard during the day as well, scanning the street, the parking lot, and even the bank lobby with a level of attention that exhausted him. He knew, rationally, that he was in a safe place, yet he was unable to relax there. The effort of keeping himself ready seemed to follow him everywhere, including into his own home, where he had expected to feel most settled.

He spoke most painfully about what the memory meant to him. Remembering the accident brought back the same terror he had felt at the time, but also an intense guilt that could come over him in a rush when he least expected it. He believed, with a seriousness that was hard to soften, that he had failed in a fundamental way. He had come to see himself as inadequate, someone who should have been more careful, more alert, less ordinary in his mistake. At times he said he felt permanently changed for the worse, as if the person he had been before the accident no longer fully existed. He judged his reactions since then harshly, taking his sleeplessness, his watchfulness, and his difficulty settling as proof that he was a lousy coper. Even as his wife reassured him, he seemed to measure himself against an ideal of steadiness he no longer believed he could meet.

Over time, these reactions made ordinary life feel smaller. He remained at work, but the bank teller role that had once suited his preference for predictability now required more effort, especially when customers came close without warning or when the day became hectic. At home, his wife noticed how often he stayed stiffly alert rather than resting, and he became quieter about what was bothering him. What finally brought Martin for help was a recent stretch of poor sleep and a sense that he could no longer keep pretending that his vigilance was simply caution. He was not seeking to erase what happened, he said, but he was afraid that the event had permanently altered him into someone who could never fully trust himself again. At the same time, he was hoping, almost cautiously, that speaking about it might help him understand why the terror and guilt still arrived with such force and whether he might ever feel safe enough to let his guard down.
